sources.entry: C: _Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast_

summary.title: Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast
summary.one_liner: Learn how Thompson's NFA simulation matches regular expressions in linear time, avoiding the exponential blowup of backtracking engines like Perl's, with a small C implementation.
keywords: build a regex engine in c
takeaways: Backtracking regex engines such as Perl, Python, PCRE and Ruby can take exponential time on patterns like a?^n a^n, while Thompson's NFA simulation stays polynomial (O(mn)).
Regular expressions map to NFAs with one state per literal or metacharacter, built by composing fragments with concatenation, alternation, and repetition constructions.
Simulating an NFA by tracking the set of reachable states at each step reads the input once and avoids trying every path.
The article gives a compact C implementation (under 400 lines) using postfix notation, a fragment stack, and state lists with a generation counter to avoid duplicates.
Backreferences make regex matching non-regular and costly; engines could use the faster algorithm for patterns without them.
summary.summary: Russ Cox walks through the theory of regular expressions, finite automata, and Ken Thompson's 1968 NFA-simulation algorithm. He explains how regexes compile to NFAs, contrasts backtracking with simultaneous state-set simulation, and presents a small portable ANSI C implementation. The article benchmarks that implementation against Perl, PCRE, Python, Ruby and others on the pathological pattern a?^n a^n, showing exponential slowdown in backtracking engines versus near-linear behavior in the NFA approach. It closes by noting how the NFA can be viewed as an on-the-fly DFA construction.
